column1: It's sunny and it's twenty-five degrees.
column2: Hace sol y estamos a veinticinco grados.
column3: both at once: impersonal hace + noun, and estar a + temperature (literally we are at)

column1: Today it's five degrees below zero.
column2: Hoy estamos a cinco grados bajo cero.
column3: bajo cero = below zero · estar a puts us on the thermometer: Spanish says we where English says it

column1: In Stockholm it's ten degrees below zero.
column2: En Estocolmo hace diez grados bajo cero.
column3: hace + degrees is the fully impersonal alternative to estamos a - both are correct

column2: La máxima de hoy es de veintiocho grados.
column3: la máxima / la mínima · measurements take ser de
lit. at how many degrees are we

column2: Estamos a tres grados sobre cero.
column3: sobre cero = above zero · the same estamos a as with dates: estamos a 15 de mayo

column2: Hoy hace más frío que ayer.
column3: más frío que = colder than

column1: It's cloudy but it isn't cold.
column2: Está nublado pero no hace frío.
column3: estar + adjective vs hacer + noun, side by side

column2: Hay niebla y hace mucho viento.
column3: hay + noun vs hacer + noun · mucho viento, not muy viento
nevar is impersonal - always third person singular

column1: The score is two to zero.
column2: El resultado es dos a cero.
column3: cero = zero

column1: There are fifteen students in the class.
column2: Hay quince estudiantes en la clase.
column3: 11-15 are one word: once, doce, trece, catorce, quince

column1: My brother is sixteen years old.
column3: 16-19 contract: dieciséis, diecisiete...
veintiuno drops to veintiún before a masculine noun
from 31 up it's three words, and uno → un

column1: There are thirty-one girls at the school.
column2: Hay treinta y una chicas en el colegio.
column3: feminine noun → treinta y una

column1: I work forty hours a week.
column3: cuarenta = 40

column1: There are fifty people at the party.
column2: Hay cincuenta personas en la fiesta.
column3: cincuenta = 50
setenta y cinco = 75

column2: Mi abuelo tiene ochenta y siete años.
column3: ochenta y siete = 87

column1: The flight costs one hundred euros.
column3: exactly 100 before a noun is cien, never ciento

column1: There are one hundred and twenty people.
column3: 101-199 use ciento, and there is no y after it

column1: The hotel has two hundred rooms.
column3: the hundreds agree in gender: doscientas habitaciones

column1: This book has five hundred pages.
column3: 500 is quinientos, not 'cincocientos'

column1: The car costs seven hundred euros.
column3: 700 is setecientos, not 'sietecientos'
900 is novecientos, not 'nuevecientos'

column1: I earn one thousand five hundred euros a month.
column2: Gano mil quinientos euros al mes.
column3: mil stands alone - never un mil

column1: The town has two thousand inhabitants.
column2: El pueblo tiene dos mil habitantes.
column3: mil never pluralises as a number: dos mil

column1: The house costs three hundred thousand euros.
column2: La casa cuesta trescientos mil euros.
column3: trescientos mil = 300,000

column1: Madrid has more than three million inhabitants.
column2: Madrid tiene más de tres millones de habitantes.
column3: millón/millones always takes de before the noun
y cuarto = quarter past
menos + minutes counts back from the next hour
en punto = on the dot
singular es, and no article
singular es, like es la una

column1: The shop opens at nine thirty.
column2: La tienda abre a las nueve y media.
column3: a las + hour for 'at'

column1: The film starts at eight in the evening.
column2: La película empieza a las ocho de la tarde.
column3: la tarde runs until about 9pm in Spain

column1: See you at half past one.
column2: Nos vemos a la una y media.
column3: a la una - singular, because it's one o'clock
casi goes before las

column1: The bus arrives in twenty minutes.
column2: El autobús llega en veinte minutos.
column3: en + time = in (how long from now)

column2: Un café con leche, por favor.
column3: the default coffee order in Spain

column1: Can we sit on the terrace?
column3: sentarse = to sit down; la terraza = outdoor seating
pedir = to order; e → i

column1: What's the dish of the day?
column3: el plato del día = daily special
lo mismo = the same thing
menú del día = fixed-price lunch, usually three courses

column1: Could you bring a little more water?
column2: ¿Me pone un poco más de agua?
column3: me pone = the standard way to order in Spain

column1: We're going to share a dessert.
column3: compartir = to share
por separado = separately
-ísimo = really, extremely
ahora = now · mismo sharpens it to right now, this very moment

column1: The waiter brings the bill straight away.
column2: El camarero trae la cuenta enseguida.
column3: enseguida = immediately, in a moment (also spelt en seguida)
pronto = soon · it can also mean early: me levanto pronto

column1: First I have breakfast and then I have a shower.
column2: Primero desayuno y después me ducho.
column3: primero... después = first... then, for putting a routine in order
por la mañana with no clock time · with a time it's de: a las ocho de la mañana

column1: In the afternoon I work and at night I rest.
column2: Por la tarde trabajo y por la noche descanso.
column3: por la tarde / por la noche · la tarde lasts until dinner, around 9pm in Spain

column1: I always drink coffee with milk.
column3: siempre usually goes before the verb
nunca before the verb needs no no · after it, it does: no como carne nunca

column2: A veces voy al trabajo a pie.
column3: a veces = sometimes (vez → veces) · a pie = on foot
todos los días = every day, plural with the article · cada día also works

column1: What subjects do you have today?
column3: la asignatura = school subject
las matemáticas is plural · los lunes = on Mondays (every week)
a subject as the subject of the sentence takes the article: la historia

column1: Physical education is my favourite subject.
column2: La educación física es mi asignatura favorita.
column3: favorita agrees with asignatura, not with the sport
languages are lowercase and take no article after estudiar

column1: My English teacher is from London.
column2: Mi profesor de inglés es de Londres.
column3: profesor de + subject = the teacher of that subject

column1: The Spanish class starts at nine.
column2: La clase de español empieza a las nueve.
column3: la clase de español · empezar e → ie

column1: Philosophy is difficult, but I like it.
column2: La filosofía es difícil, pero me gusta.
column3: gusta singular because la filosofía is one thing

column1: I like maths, but I don't like history.
column2: Me gustan las matemáticas, pero no me gusta la historia.
column3: gustan for the plural matemáticas, gusta for la historia

column2: El recreo es a las once.
column3: el recreo = break / playtime · events take ser + a las

column2: A mis amigos les gusta la música.
column3: naming the person takes both halves: a + person, and the pronoun stays · les matches mis amigos, gusta matches la música

column2: A Ana le gusta el café.
column3: one person → le · a Ana, never just Ana

column2: A mis padres les gusta viajar.
column3: les for the people, gusta for the infinitive (an infinitive counts as singular)

column2: A mí me gusta este restaurante.
column3: a mí adds emphasis (I'm the one who likes it) · me still can't be dropped

column2: ¿A ti te gustan las películas españolas?
column3: a plural thing → gustan, whoever is doing the liking

column2: A mi hermano no le gusta el pescado.
column3: no goes before the pronoun: no le gusta

column2: A los niños les gustan los animales.
column3: plural people → les, plural thing → gustan: both change here

column1: My sister likes dogs, but I don't.
column2: A mi hermana le gustan los perros, pero a mí no.
column3: a mí no is the whole answer - the verb isn't repeated

column2: A todos les gusta la playa.
column3: todos is plural → les
even a question word takes a + le

column1: Do you all like the book?
column3: os = to you all, the vosotros pronoun · you'll hear it constantly in Spain and almost never in Latin America

column1: Do you all like Spanish films?
column3: os + gustan because películas is plural · the pronoun never changes for the number of things
an infinitive counts as one thing → gusta, even with two verbs after it

column1: We don't like getting up early.
column3: the infinitive keeps its own reflexive pronoun: levantarnos, matching nos
te + gustan · Spanish keeps the article: los gatos, not just gatos

column2: Nací en mil novecientos ochenta y cinco.
column3: a year is read as one whole number, never split in two like nineteen eighty-five · nacer = to be born

column2: Nació en mil novecientos noventa y cinco.
column3: mil stands alone: never un mil
en qué año · naciste = you were born

column1: In the year 2000 I lived in Madrid.
column2: En el año dos mil viví en Madrid.
column3: 2000 = dos mil · el año is usual before a round year
estamos en + year, the same estamos as with dates and temperatures

column2: Colón llegó en mil cuatrocientos noventa y dos.
column3: the 1400s start with mil cuatrocientos · en + year, with no article

column2: Vivo aquí desde dos mil diecinueve.
column3: desde + year · the plain present covers English's have lived

column2: El curso empieza en dos mil veintiséis.
column3: dos mil veintiséis · veintiséis keeps its accent

column1: My daughter was born on the 3rd of May 2010.
column2: Mi hija nació el tres de mayo de dos mil diez.
column3: a full date is el + number + de + month + de + year · months are lowercase

column1: In the nineties there was no internet.
column2: En los años noventa no había internet.
column3: los años noventa = the nineties · había = there was / there were

column1: Do you see the book? - Yes, I see it.
column3: lo stands in for el libro · the pronoun goes before the verb

column1: Do you have the keys? - Yes, I have them.
column3: las llaves is feminine plural → las

column1: Do you buy the newspaper? - Yes, I buy it every day.
column2: ¿Compras el periódico? - Sí, lo compro todos los días.
column3: lo = el periódico · it never disappears the way English drops it
no goes first, then the pronoun, then the verb
me = me · still in front of the verb

column1: Do you eat meat? - No, I don't eat it.
column3: la = la carne · the gender comes from the noun, not from the thing

column1: Do you know my sister? - Yes, I know her.
column2: ¿Conoces a mi hermana? - Sí, la conozco.
column3: the personal a in the question, la for her in the answer

column1: I'm going to do it tomorrow.
column3: with an infinitive you may also say lo voy a hacer - both are correct
attached to the infinitive: llamarme · ¿me puedes llamar? works just as well

column1: I don't want to see it.
column3: no + conjugated verb, and the pronoun rides on the infinitive

column1: Where are the tickets? I don't have them.
column2: ¿Dónde están las entradas? No las tengo.
column3: la entrada = ticket · las tengo, never tengo las
le is for the person receiving it
le + lo is impossible, so le becomes se: se lo doy

column1: They invite us to the party.
column3: nos = us
escuchar takes the object directly: no a, no to

column1: I always tell her the truth.
column3: le = to her · decir takes the person as le, the thing as the object

column1: The teacher explains the lesson to us.
column2: El profesor nos explica la lección.
column3: nos = to us · explicar works like decir
te = for you · Spanish needs no word for for here

column1: She writes to them every week.
column3: les = to them, even though the people aren't named

column1: Can you lend me ten euros?
column3: prestar = to lend · me = to me
mandar / enviar = to send

column1: The book is on the table.
column2: El libro está encima de la mesa.
column3: encima de = on top of · sobre la mesa works too

column1: The cat is under the chair.
column2: El gato está debajo de la silla.
column3: debajo de = under

column1: The pharmacy is next to the bank.
column2: La farmacia está al lado del banco.
column3: al lado de + el → del

column1: The supermarket is opposite the school.
column2: El supermercado está enfrente del colegio.
column3: enfrente de = opposite, facing

column1: My house is between the park and the church.
column2: Mi casa está entre el parque y la iglesia.
column3: entre takes no de

column1: The car is in front of the house.
column2: El coche está delante de la casa.
column3: delante de = in front of

column1: The garden is behind the house.
column2: El jardín está detrás de la casa.
column3: detrás de = behind

column1: The bathroom is at the end of the corridor.
column2: El baño está al final del pasillo.
column3: al final de = at the end of · el pasillo = corridor

column1: The station is far from the centre.
column2: La estación está lejos del centro.
column3: lejos de ↔ cerca de

column1: The keys are inside the bag.
column2: Las llaves están dentro del bolso.
column3: dentro de = inside · el bolso = bag
fuera on its own needs no de

column1: Is there a pharmacy near here?
column3: hay to ask whether something exists · por aquí cerca = round here
doler works backwards like gustar · la cabeza, not mi cabeza
a plural body part → duelen
Spanish says the throat hurts me
el estómago keeps its accent
tener + fiebre, with no article
estar for a passing state · resfriada if you're female
encontrarse = to feel · no me siento bien also works
the everyday question when someone is ill
lit. what happens to you

column1: I need to go to the doctor.
column3: ir al médico = to go to the doctor's
the colour follows the noun and agrees with it
blanco → blanca for a feminine noun
masculine plural: blancos
verde has no separate feminine: just add -s
azul → azules · gustan for a plural thing
gris is the same for both genders
marrón → marrones in the plural

column1: The black trousers are on the bed.
column2: Los pantalones negros están encima de la cama.
column3: pantalones is plural in Spanish → negros

column2: Mi color favorito es el amarillo.
column3: a colour on its own takes el: el amarillo
de qué color, with de
from Emerson Fittipaldi, F1 champion in 1972 and 1974, spelt the Spanish way with one t · someone who goes fast, happily and a bit madly - it's affectionate, not a warning

column1: Slow down, you're not a racing driver!
column3: que opens a friendly reproach and barely translates · más despacio = slower

column1: What time do you start your first class on Monday?
column2: ¿A qué hora empiezas la primera clase el lunes?
column3: a qué hora = at what time · el lunes = this coming Monday; los lunes = every Monday

column1: My first class starts at a quarter past eight.
column2: Mi primera clase empieza a las ocho y cuarto.
column3: empezar: e → ie · y cuarto = quarter past

column1: How many minutes is one lesson?
column3: durar = to last, the natural verb here - Spanish asks how long a class lasts, not how many minutes it is
cada + singular noun, never cada clases

column1: Which subjects do you have this year?
column3: qué + noun for which · este año = this year

column1: How many Spanish classes do you have a week?
column2: ¿Cuántas clases de español tienes a la semana?
column3: cuántas agrees with clases · a la semana = per week (por semana works too)

column1: I have three Spanish classes a week.
column2: Tengo tres clases de español a la semana.
column3: clase de + subject, and the subject stays lowercase
cuál + ser to pick one out of a set · ¿qué asignatura...? also works

column2: Mi asignatura favorita es la historia.
column3: the subject keeps its article after es: la historia

column1: What time do you usually finish?
column3: terminar = to finish (acabar works the same) · normalmente sits after the verb

column1: I usually finish at half past two.
column2: Normalmente termino a las dos y media.
column3: normalmente can also open the sentence · y media = half past

column1: Classes finish at three in the afternoon.
column2: Las clases terminan a las tres de la tarde.
column3: de la tarde with a clock time; por la tarde without one
